title: QUANTIFIERS
notes:
✓ Quantifiers → words or phrases used before nouns to show quantity or amount.

✓ Examples → some, any, much, many, a lot of, few, little, several, enough, all, both, each, every, no.

✓ I have some money.
✓ There are many students.
✓ We don't have much time.

✓ The correct quantifier depends mainly on whether the noun is countable or uncountable.

title: COUNTABLE & UNCOUNTABLE NOUNS
notes:
✓ Countable nouns → can be counted individually and have singular/plural forms.

✓ one book → two books
✓ one student → many students
✓ one apple → several apples

✓ Uncountable nouns → are treated as substances, materials, concepts, or masses and normally do not have a plural form.

✓ water, money, information, advice, furniture, rice, knowledge, traffic

◆ Countable → many, few, several, each, every.
◆ Uncountable → much, little, a little.
◆ Both → some, any, a lot of, lots of, enough, plenty of, all, no.

title: SOME
notes:
✓ Some → an unspecified amount or number; commonly used in affirmative statements.

✓ I have some money.
✓ She bought some books.
✓ There is some water in the bottle.

✓ Some can be used with both countable plural and uncountable nouns.

◆ some + plural countable noun
◆ some + uncountable noun

✓ some students
✓ some information

title: ANY
notes:
✓ Any → commonly used in questions and negative statements.

✓ Do you have any money?
✓ I don't have any money.
✓ Are there any students in the room?

✓ Any can be used with plural countable and uncountable nouns.

✓ In affirmative sentences, any can mean 'it does not matter which/what'.
✓ You can choose any book.

title: SOME VS ANY
notes:
✓ SOME → commonly affirmative.
✓ I have some friends.

✓ ANY → commonly questions and negatives.
✓ Do you have any friends?
✓ I don't have any friends.

✓ SOME can also be used in offers and requests when expecting or encouraging a positive response.

✓ Would you like some coffee?
✓ Could I have some water?

✓ Basic rule → some = positive; any = questions/negatives, with important exceptions.

title: MUCH
notes:
✓ Much → a large amount of an uncountable noun.

✓ I don't have much money.
✓ How much water do you need?
✓ There isn't much time left.

✓ Much + uncountable noun.

⚠ Much is especially common in questions and negative sentences.

✓ How much information do you need?
✓ We don't have much time.

✓ In affirmative everyday speech, a lot of/lots of is often more natural.

title: MANY
notes:
✓ Many → a large number of plural countable nouns.

✓ There are many students here.
✓ She has many books.
✓ How many people came?

✓ Many + plural countable noun.

⚠ Do not use many directly with an uncountable noun.

❌ many information
✓ much information
✓ a lot of information

title: A LOT OF / LOTS OF
notes:
✓ A lot of / lots of → a large quantity or number; used with both countable and uncountable nouns.

✓ She has a lot of friends.
✓ We have a lot of work.
✓ There are lots of students here.
✓ He drinks lots of water.

◆ a lot of + plural countable noun.
◆ a lot of + uncountable noun.

✓ Lots of is slightly more informal.

title: FEW & A FEW
notes:
✓ Few → a small number; emphasizes that the number is insufficient or less than expected.

✓ Few students understood the question.
→ Almost none understood it.

✓ A few → a small number, but enough or some are available.

✓ A few students understood the question.
→ Some students understood it.

✓ FEW → negative idea.
✓ A FEW → positive/neutral idea.

⚠ Both are used with plural countable nouns.

title: LITTLE & A LITTLE
notes:
✓ Little → a small amount; emphasizes that the amount is insufficient.

✓ There is little water left.
→ Almost no water remains.

✓ A little → a small amount that exists and may be enough.

✓ There is a little water left.
→ Some water remains.

✓ LITTLE → negative idea.
✓ A LITTLE → positive/neutral idea.

⚠ Both are used with uncountable nouns.

title: FEW VS LITTLE
notes:
✓ FEW → plural countable nouns.
✓ few books
✓ few students
✓ few opportunities

✓ LITTLE → uncountable nouns.
✓ little money
✓ little time
✓ little water

✓ Memory trick →
FEW → things you can COUNT.
LITTLE → things you measure as an AMOUNT.

title: SEVERAL
notes:
✓ Several → more than two but not a large number; exact quantity is not specified.

✓ I have visited several countries.
✓ Several students were absent.
✓ She asked several questions.

✓ Several + plural countable noun.

⚠ Do not use several with uncountable nouns.

❌ several money
✓ several amounts of money

title: ENOUGH
notes:
✓ Enough → means as much/as many as necessary.

✓ We have enough food.
✓ There are enough chairs.
✓ I have enough money.

◆ enough + noun
✓ enough time
✓ enough students

✓ With adjectives/adverbs → adjective/adverb + enough.
✓ She is old enough to drive.
✓ He ran quickly enough to catch the bus.

⚠ Not → enough + adjective.
❌ enough old
✓ old enough

title: PLENTY OF
notes:
✓ Plenty of → more than enough; emphasizes that there is a sufficient or abundant amount.

✓ We have plenty of time.
✓ There are plenty of opportunities.
✓ She has plenty of money.

✓ Used with both countable and uncountable nouns.

✓ plenty of students
✓ plenty of water

✓ Meaning → more than enough.

title: NO & NONE
notes:
✓ No → used directly before a noun and means 'not any'.

✓ There is no water.
✓ I have no money.
✓ There are no students here.

✓ None → used without a following noun, often with 'of'.

✓ None of the students came.
✓ None of the water was clean.

✓ Compare:
✓ I have no money.
✓ I have none.
✓ None of my friends came.

title: ALL
notes:
✓ All → refers to the whole quantity or number of something.

✓ All students must attend.
✓ All the water has disappeared.
✓ All of my friends came.

✓ Used with plural countable nouns and uncountable nouns.

◆ all + plural noun
◆ all + uncountable noun
◆ all of + determiner/pronoun + noun

✓ all of the students
✓ all of the money

title: BOTH
notes:
✓ Both → refers to two people or things together.

✓ Both students passed.
✓ Both of my brothers are doctors.
✓ Both answers are correct.

✓ Both + plural countable noun.
✓ Both of + determiner/pronoun + plural noun.

⚠ Both refers specifically to two, not three or more.

title: EACH & EVERY
notes:
✓ Each → considers members individually.
✓ Each student received a book.

✓ Every → considers members as a group of individuals.
✓ Every student must attend.

✓ Both are followed by a singular countable noun and usually take a singular verb.

✓ Each student is ready.
✓ Every student is ready.

⚠ Do not normally say 'every students'.
❌ Every students are ready.
✓ Every student is ready.

title: EACH VS EVERY
notes:
✓ EACH → emphasizes individual members and can be used with two or more.
✓ Each student received a different number.

✓ EVERY → refers to all members individually but as part of a group; normally used with three or more.
✓ Every student in the class passed.

◆ Common patterns:
✓ each of + plural noun/pronoun
✓ every + singular noun

✓ Each of the students has a book.
✓ Every student has a book.

title: A NUMBER OF & THE NUMBER OF
notes:
✓ A number of + plural noun → means 'many/several' and takes a plural verb.

✓ A number of students are absent.

✓ The number of + plural noun → refers to the total number and takes a singular verb.

✓ The number of students is increasing.

✓ KEY DIFFERENCE:
A NUMBER OF → plural verb.
THE NUMBER OF → singular verb.

title: TOO MUCH & TOO MANY
notes:
✓ Too much → more than is desirable/necessary + uncountable noun.

✓ There is too much sugar in the tea.
✓ I have too much work.

✓ Too many → more than is desirable/necessary + plural countable noun.

✓ There are too many people here.
✓ He made too many mistakes.

✓ MUCH → uncountable.
✓ MANY → plural countable.

title: SO MUCH & SO MANY
notes:
✓ So much → a very large amount.
✓ There is so much water.

✓ So many → a very large number.
✓ There are so many students.

✓ SO MUCH + uncountable noun.
✓ SO MANY + plural countable noun.

✓ I have so much work to do.
✓ She has so many books.

title: QUANTIFIER + OF
notes:
✓ Many quantifiers can be followed by 'of' before a determiner such as the, my, these, or a pronoun.

✓ many students
✓ many of the students

✓ some books
✓ some of the books

✓ all students
✓ all of the students

✓ each student
✓ each of the students

✓ none of the students

✓ Pattern → quantifier + of + determiner/pronoun + noun.

title: COMMON ERRORS
notes:
❌ much students
✓ many students

❌ many information
✓ much information

❌ few money
✓ little money

❌ a little students
✓ a few students

❌ every students
✓ every student

❌ each students
✓ each student

❌ I don't have some money.
✓ I don't have any money.

❌ There are much people here.
✓ There are many people here.

❌ The number of students are increasing.
✓ The number of students is increasing.

❌ A number of students is absent.
✓ A number of students are absent.

title: EXAM GUIDE
notes:
◆ 1. COUNTABLE PLURAL → many, few, a few, several, both.

◆ 2. UNCOUNTABLE → much, little, a little.

◆ 3. BOTH TYPES → some, any, a lot of, lots of, enough, plenty of, all, no.

◆ 4. Large amount → much / a lot of / plenty of.

◆ 5. Large number → many / a lot of / plenty of.

◆ 6. Small number → few / a few.

◆ 7. Small amount → little / a little.

◆ 8. Negative/insufficient idea → few / little.

◆ 9. Some but not much/many → a few / a little.

◆ 10. Prohibition/absence → no.

◆ 11. 'Not necessary amount' → enough.

◆ 12. More than necessary → too much / too many.

✓ Golden rule → Always identify whether the noun is singular countable, plural countable, or uncountable before choosing the quantifier.
